## _gtypes_ objects

For most functions in _strataG_, you will need to load your data into a _gtypes_ object. A _gtypes_ object is an R S4 class with several slots that are fully described in `?gtypes`. However, unless you fully know what you are doing, it is not advised that you try to create _gtypes_ objects or extract information from them directly. Several utility functions have been provided to make this process easier which will be described and demonstrated below.  

First, let's look at how one can read raw genetic data into R and how it should be formatted.  

### Genotypic Data

It is easiest to load raw genotype data from a text file, for example saved in comma-delimited (.CSV) format. The standard R functions _read.table()_ or _read.csv()_ can be used to accomplish this. However, in _strataG_, the _readGenData()_ function has been provided for reading data from .CSV files. This is a wrapper for _data.table::fread()_ that sets commonly used values for missing data and removes blank lines.

```{r}
gen.data <- readGenData("msats.csv")
str(gen.data)
```

Genetic data should have one column per allele at a locus. Columns for multiple alleles in the same locus (e.g., diploid data) should be next to each other and have the same column name, but differ in suffix (e.g., "Locus.1", "Locus.2" or "LocA", "LocB"). A column of individual identifiers should be the first column.  

### Sequence Data  

For sequence data stored in FASTA format, the _read.fasta()_ function is available, which is a wrapper for the _read.dna()_ function in the _ape_ package with standard FASTA arguments set. This will create a DNAbin object in the workspace:

```{r}
fname <- system.file("extdata/dolph.seqs.fasta", package = "strataG")
dolph.seqs <- read.fasta(fname) 
dolph.seqs
```

For sequences stored in other formats, _read.dna()_ should be used directly.

### Stratification schemes

If desired, individuals can also be stratified to different populations. The suggested way to manage this is to create a spreadsheet that has one row per individual. The first column should contain sample identifiers. Every column thereafter specifies a stratification "scheme". The values in each of the columns identify which stratum the individual in that row belongs to in that scheme. Multiple schemes can be defined. If some individuals are not to be involved in analyses of a given scheme, that is, they are unstratified, the value for that scheme should be left blank.

```{r}
schemes <- readGenData('schemes.csv')
str(schemes)
head(schemes)
tail(schemes)
```

### Creating a _gtypes_ object (_df2gtypes_)

The easiest way to create a _gtypes_ object is with the _df2gtypes()_ function. To use this function, you have to have loaded the genetic data as a matrix or data.frame in the workspace. By default, the function assumes that the first column in the data contains the individual identifiers, the second column contains population stratifications, and third column and all columns thereafter contain allelic data.

Here is an example constructing such a data.frame with the example microsatellite data and the stratification schemes. Throughout this tutorial, we'll use functions from the _tidyverse_ to manipulate the data.frames: 

```{r}
schemes <- readGenData('schemes.csv')
gen.data <- readGenData("msats.csv")

gen.df <- schemes |> 
  select(id, region) |> 
  left_join(gen.data, by = 'id')

str(gen.df)
```

We then create a _gtypes_ object with this data.frame, specifying that it is diploid data (_ploidy = 2_).

```{r}
msats.g <- df2gtypes(
  gen.df,
  ploidy = 2
)

msats.g
```

Note that any individuals without data are dropped from the created _gtypes_ object.

If you wish to restratify individuals for some analyses, you can optionally include the stratification scheme to the object when creating it by supplying the data.frame to the _schemes_ argument. You can also include a meaningful description to the _gtypes_ object that will get used in labelling some output:

```{r}
msats.g <- df2gtypes(
  gen.df,
  ploidy = 2,
  schemes = schemes,
  description = "Example microsatellite data"
)

msats.g
```

Haploid data would be created in the same way:

```{r}
# grab first allele of first locus to simulate haploid data

#' note that we can use pipes here to read the data directly and 
#' create a gtypes object in the same pipeline

hap.g <- readGenData('schemes.csv') |> 
  select(id, ecotype) |> 
  left_join(
    select(readGenData("msats.csv"), id, D11t.1), 
    by = 'id'
  ) |> 
  df2gtypes(
    ploidy = 1, 
    description = 'haploid example'
  )

hap.g
```

If the haplotypes are associated with sequences (e.g., mtDNA), the sequences are included in creating the _gtypes_ object. If the sequence names are the same as the individual ids, then just replicate that column in the data.frame passed to _df2gtypes_ (but make sure to give the new column a different name).

If haplotypes are missing in the sequences provided, an error is thrown and the _gtypes_ object won't be created. In this case, we also need to remove those rows before creating the object.

```{r}
seq.df <- schemes |> 
  # we just need the id and strata assignments
  select(id, region) |>  
  # add a new column for the sequence ids
  mutate(dLoop = id) |>
  # remove ids without sequences
  filter(dLoop %in% names(dolph.seqs)) 

dolph.seqs <- read.fasta(
  system.file("extdata/dolph.seqs.fasta", package = "strataG")
) 

seqs.g <- df2gtypes(
  seq.df,
  ploidy = 1,
  sequences = dolph.seqs,
  schemes = schemes,
  description = 'Dolphin mtDNA sequences'
)

seqs.g
```

Note that since each sequence in _dolph.seqs_ is for a given individual, the _num.ind_ and _num.haplotypes_ values are the same for both strata. In order to convert the sequences to unique haplotypes, use the _labelHaplotypes()_ function:

```{r}
haps.g <- labelHaplotypes(seqs.g)
haps.g
```

### Creating a _gtypes_ object directly from sequences   (_sequence2gtypes_)

The _sequence2gtypes()_ function creates an unstratified _gtype_ object with just a set of DNA sequences:
```{r}
seqs.g <- sequence2gtypes(dolph.seqs)
seqs.g
```

If you have a vector that identifies strata designations for the sequences, that can be supplied as well:  
```{r}
# extract the stratifications, remove unstratified individuals
eco.strata <- schemes |> 
  select(id, ecotype) |> 
  filter(!is.na(ecotype)) |> 
  deframe()

tail(eco.strata)
```

```{r}
# create the gtypes object
seqs.g <- sequence2gtypes(
  dolph.seqs, 
  strata = eco.strata, 
  seq.names = "dLoop",
  description = "dLoop: ecotype stratification"
)

seqs.g
```

## Conversions from other packages.

There are conversion functions for data objects from several other popular packages in R, such as _adegenet_(genind), _pegas_(loci), and _phangorn_(phydat).
```{r}
library(adegenet)
# from example(df2genind)
df <- data.frame(locusA=c("11","11","12","32"),
                 locusB=c(NA,"34","55","15"),
                 locusC=c("22","22","21","22"))
row.names(df) <- .genlab("genotype",4)
obj <- df2genind(df, ploidy=2, ncode=1)
obj

# convert to gtypes
gi.g <- genind2gtypes(obj)
gi.g
```

## Accessor functions

There are several functions for getting basic information from a _gtypes_ object (see `?accessors`):

* __getNumInd(g)__ The number of individuals.
* __getNumLoci(g)__ The number of loci.
* __getNumStrata(g)__ The number of strata in the current scheme.
* __getIndNames(g)__ The names of the individuals.
* __getLociNames(g)__ The names of the loci or genes.
* __getStrataNames(g)__ The names of the strata in the current scheme.
* __getPloidy(g)__ The ploidy of each locus.
* __getStrata(g)__ The current strata to which each individual belongs.
* __getSchemes(g)__ A data frame of potential stratification schemes.
* __getSequences(g)__ The sequences stored in a haploid object.
* __getDescription(g)__ The text description of the object.
* __getOther(g)__ The list used to store other information about the object.

Some functions are available for modifying values in the object as well, such as:

* __setStrata(g)__ Replace the vector of strata assignments.
* __setSchemes(g)__ Replace the data.frame of potential stratification schemes.
* __setDescription(g)__ Replace the label describing the object.
* __setOther(g)__ Replace the optional data stored in the \@other slot.

## Subsetting/Indexing

A _gtypes_ object can be subset using the standard R '[' indexing operation, with three slots: [i, j, k]. The first (i) specifies the desired individuals, the second (j) is the loci to return, and the third (k) is the strata. All standard R indexing operations involving numerical, character, or logical vectors work for each argument.  

For example, to return a _gtypes_ object containing 5 random individuals from the example microsatellite data provided in the package:
```{r}
# get 10 random ids
ran.ids <- sample(getNumInd(msats.g), 5)
head(ran.ids)

# index to extract
sub.msats <- msats.g[ran.ids, , ]
sub.msats
```

...or to return specific loci:
```{r}
sub.msats <- sub.msats[, c("D11t", "EV37", "TV7"), ]
sub.msats
```

...or some loci in a specific stratum:
```{r}
sub.msats <- msats.g[, c("Ttr11", "D11t"), "Coastal"]
sub.msats
```

## Stratifying samples

You can specify the stratification scheme when creating a _gtypes_ object as in the examples above. Once a _gtypes_ object has been created, you can also change the stratification scheme by either supplying a new vector for the strata slot:
```{r}
# randomly stratify individuals to two populations
msats <- msats.g
new.strata <- sample(c("Pop1", "Pop2"), getNumInd(msats), rep = TRUE)
names(new.strata) <- getIndNames(msats)
setStrata(msats) <- new.strata
msats
```

or, if there is a stratification scheme data.frame in the schemes slot, you can use the _stratify_ function to choose a stratification scheme:
```{r}
# choose "broad" stratification scheme
msats <- stratify(msats, "ecotype")
msats
```

You can update the schemes with a data.frame like this:
```{r}
new.schemes <- getSchemes(msats)
new.schemes$inner.outer <- sample(
  c("Inner", "Outer", NA), 
  nrow(new.schemes), 
  rep = TRUE
)
setSchemes(msats) <- new.schemes
```

NOTE: Filling or changing the schemes slot does not affect the current stratification of the samples. You must then select a new stratification scheme or fill the strata slot as above.
```{r}
msats.inner.outer <- stratify(msats, "inner.outer")
msats.inner.outer
```

You can also randomly permute the current stratification scheme using the _permuteStrata()_ function like this:
```{r}
msats <- stratify(msats, "offshore")

# original
msats

# permuted
ran.msats <- permuteStrata(msats)
ran.msats
```
NOTE: Only samples assigned to strata are permuted with _permuteStrata_. Those not assigned (NAs) remain unassigned.

## Exporting

The allelic data in a _gtypes_ object can be converted back to a matrix or data frame with _as.matrix()_ and _as.data.frame()_:
```{r}
gen.mat <- as.matrix(msats)
head(gen.mat)
```

By default, this function splits each allele into its own column. One can make a matrix with one locus per column and alleles separated by a specified character by setting the _one.col_ argument to _TRUE_:
```{r}
gen.mat <- as.matrix(msats, one.col = TRUE)
head(gen.mat)
```

See other options for output in _?as.data.frame.gtypes_.  

The contents of a _gtypes_ object can be written to a file with the _writeGtypes()_ function. This will write a .csv file with the allelic information and a .fasta file for any sequence data if it exists.
